title: A per-case error scatter asks which targets the surrogate model can be trusted for, and whether it is as good where the search goes as on fresh points
summary: Each dot is one target. The log y axis shows the worst relative error of the surrogate against the full simulation, for two kinds of points. Most cases sit near or below 1 percent, a few are far worse, and the testing set is usually worse than the points the search actually visited.

media.alt: Scatter plot titled Tig targets. Case ID from 0 to 90 on the x axis, relative maximum residual error in percent on a log y axis from 0.01 to 10. Blue dots for search iterations and orange dots for testing data. Between about 25 and 45 the two sets overlap close to 0.1 percent. Several orange dots in the first twenty cases rise to 2 to 9 percent. No points between cases 46 and 54.

read_the_figure.question: For each target, how large is the surrogate model's worst-case error on the search path and on independent points?
read_the_figure.axes: x: case identifier (one integer per target). y: relative maximum residual error in percent on a logarithmic axis. Blue: points visited by the genetic-algorithm search. Orange: independent testing data.
look_at: Vertical gap between blue and orange for the same case. Where orange is far above blue, the surrogate was accurate where the search went and inaccurate on test points.
Cases where the two colours overlap, for example around cases 25 to 45 in figure 23: the surrogate is equally good on both and close to 0.1 percent.
Outliers. In figure 23 a handful of orange dots rise to the 2 to 9 percent range in the first twenty cases. In figure 24 (flame speed) some orange dots reach tens of percent for a few cases.
Gaps in case numbering, such as 20 to 25 and 46 to 54 in figure 23. These cases have no point, which means they were skipped, filtered, or not part of the study. The figure does not say.
Compare 23 and 24. Flame-speed targets have a wider spread of errors than ignition-delay targets, so the surrogate is less uniform for them.
read_the_figure.proves: That for most targets the surrogate's worst-case error is small enough to substitute for the simulation in the search, and flags the targets where it is not. It does not show the error at the optimum, which may lie off the search path.
if_wrong: Orange systematically above blue: the surrogate was fitted on a region that the testing set samples differently. Expect extrapolation error.
Blue above orange: the search is wandering into regions the testing set misses.
A band of very high errors for a block of cases: those targets are poorly captured by the polynomial form.
All points the same height: the metric is saturated or the model is trivial.
must_check: The metric is defined (maximum over which points, relative to which value).
The y axis is log and starts at a value below the smallest point.
The number of points behind each dot is stated.
Training data are not mixed with testing data in the orange set.

terms.meaning: Prediction minus truth, divided by the truth, usually quoted in percent.
The largest absolute relative error over a set of points. It is a worst case, not an average.
The parameter sets that the genetic-algorithm search visited. The surrogate is judged on the regions the optimizer actually explores.
Samples held out from the fit and used only to measure the surrogate's accuracy.
A polynomial in the parameters fitted to simulation results, used in place of the simulation.
Testing error minus training error. It measures how much the surrogate overfits.
An axis where equal distances are equal ratios. Here one gridline interval is a factor of ten in error.

remember: A maximum is a worst case: it can only be larger than the mean.
On a log axis a dot at 1 is ten times higher than one at 0.1.
Testing data are expected to be worse than training data.
A good surrogate on the search path is what the optimizer needs.
Gaps in case numbers need an explanation.

steps.title: Relative error at one point
steps.note: Prediction of the surrogate minus the simulated value, divided by the simulated value. It is dimensionless and quoted in percent.

steps.title: The plotted quantity for one case and one set
steps.note: The figure label says relative maximum residual error: the maximum over the points of a set S (search iterations or testing data), in percent. The exact definition is inferred from the axis title.

steps.title: Why a maximum is larger than a mean
steps.note: So a dot at 1 percent hides that most points in that set are much better. It also grows with the number of points, because more points means a larger chance of an extreme one.

steps.title: Why training residuals are optimistic
steps.note: For a least-squares fit, the residual at a training point is shrunk by the leverage h_ii because the point pulled the fit towards itself. The error at a new point carries an extra term that grows away from the data. Hence testing error is expected to exceed training error.

steps.title: Reading a log axis
steps.note: Two dots one gridline apart differ by a factor ten. A gap of half a gridline is a factor of about 3.2.

steps.title: Why search points can be better than testing points
steps.tex: \hat y\ \text{is accurate near the data}\;\Rightarrow\;|e|\ \text{small on a concentrated search path}
steps.note: A search that converges visits a narrow region near the optimum, where the surrogate was densely sampled. A testing set spread over the whole domain contains points far from it. That asymmetry explains orange above blue.

worked.title: Reading the gap between testing and search error
worked.problem: In figure 23 one case has search error of about 2.3 percent and testing error of about 9 percent (read by eye). What factor separates them, and how many decades on the plot?
worked.answer: The testing error is about 3.9 times the search error, or about 0.6 of a decade (a little over half a gridline) on the log axis. Values were read off the figure by eye and are approximate.

analyze.q: In the first twenty cases of figure 23, orange is well above blue. In cases 25 to 45 they coincide. Suggest two reasons for the change.
analyze.hint: What do the cases represent, and how far from the data does each testing point lie?

analyze.q: Flame-speed errors in figure 24 reach tens of percent for a few cases. What would you inspect next for those cases?
analyze.hint: Their sensitivity charts and the range of parameters sampled.

analyze.q: Why do blue dots have a smaller spread than orange dots in many regions?

evaluate.q: Would you use the surrogate for the cases with the largest orange errors? Under what condition?
Is a maximum over many points a fair metric for comparing two surrogates built with different numbers of test points?

create: Redraw the figure with cases on the x axis sorted by testing error, the two sets joined by thin vertical lines, and a horizontal band marking the experimental uncertainty of the target.
Design a plot that shows, for one case, the distribution (not just the maximum) of relative errors in both sets.

checks.q: What does the y axis show?
checks.answer: The largest relative error, in percent and on a log scale, between the surrogate's prediction and the full simulation over a set of points, for each case.

checks.q: Two dots are at 0.1 and 1 percent. By what factor do they differ?
checks.answer: A factor of ten, one decade on the log axis.

checks.q: Why is testing error usually above training error?
checks.answer: The fit adapts to the training points and the training residuals are shrunk by leverage, while a new point carries extra variance from distance to the data. The gap measures overfitting.

checks.q: A case has small search error and large testing error. Is the surrogate safe for the optimization of that case?
checks.answer: Probably yes within the explored region, but not safe elsewhere. The search error is what matters while the search stays there, and a larger testing error warns against using the surrogate to predict far from that region.

checks.q: What extra column would you add to the figure so that a reader can tell whether a large maximum comes from one point or from many?
checks.answer: Add the median error of the same set, or the fraction of points above a stated tolerance, next to the maximum.

provenance.notes: Standard theory only (error metrics, train/test gap). Values are read off a log axis by eye, approximate, and only used qualitatively. The figures are spreadsheet screenshots with selection handles visible at the corners and mid-edges of figure 23, which the owner may want to re-export. The y label says Relative Maximum Residual Error (%): the exact definition (maximum over what set, relative to what) is not on the figure. The legend entry 'search iterations' means points visited by the search, not a held-out set. The cases are numbered but not named, and gaps in the numbering (for example 46 to 54 in figure 23) are not explained. Caption refers to a design matrix of a given rank; that is not explained here.
